title: AI search over a curated precedent library, under existing permissions
problem: Lawyers cannot quickly find the precedent or template they want in a growing collection; at Allens, browsing through SharePoint was meant only as an interim fix.
approach: The knowledge team curates precedents with a taxonomy; AI search surfaces them in the document system at Allens and Womble Bond Dickinson.
Insight+ search extended to 1,350 legal staff at Allens, with positive feedback and no usage or time measures (vendor-published).
Content owners curate and tag material first, and the lawyer chooses which retrieved precedent applies to the matter.
who: Allens, Womble Bond Dickinson UK, iManage

title: Asking questions of the firm's own documents to find clauses and precedents
problem: A lawyer remembers a good clause from a prior deal but loses time hunting through folders, and may land on an unexecuted draft or counterparty markup.
approach: An assistant inside the document system answers plain-language questions against the firm's own documents, at Chaffetz Lindsey and Digital Commerce Bank.
Chaffetz Lindsey deployed it within a two-month window (vendor-published); Litera claims 2-10 hours per week for its whole platform (vendor-published).
The lawyer reads the cited passage in the source and decides whether a retrieved clause fits the deal.
who: Chaffetz Lindsey, Digital Commerce Bank, iManage

title: Consulting firm's own knowledge assistant, with referral to internal experts
problem: At engagement kickoff, finding the most relevant research and experts is described as taking about two weeks of researching and networking, even for senior colleagues.
approach: McKinsey built Lilli over more than 40 curated knowledge sources; it returns relevant internal content and points users to experts.
Over 4 million prompts, about 150,000 a week, over 75% of employees had tested it; 30% time saved (all self-reported).
Consultants validate what Lilli returns, and a person reviews everything before it reaches a client.

title: Finding who has done this before from matter, people and engagement records
problem: A partner asking whether the firm has handled something similar finds the answer depends on who is in the room; expertise directories were once kept by annual survey.
approach: Lilli points McKinsey users to internal experts; Intapp, Litera and NetDocuments offer experience search, mostly as product claims, some in private preview.
Arup's CV platform engaged over 12,000 professionals and imported about 7,000 CVs; the case study does not claim AI (vendor-published).
The professional decides whom to contact, and a KM or practice leader confirms experience claims before pitching on them.

title: Reclassifying and summarising historic documents into an AI-ready knowledge bank
problem: Decades of firm work sit in repositories that generative tools cannot safely be pointed at; Clifford Chance aims for a curated set of trusted internal materials.
approach: Clifford Chance launched a Knowledge Bank with Epiq and Microsoft: 400,000+ documents reclassified and summarised, with natural-language search and permission-aware results.
It reports the document count (self-reported) but no time, cost or quality measure; no source shows lawyers using it yet.
Knowledge professionals reviewing AI classifications is a prediction from another source, not reported for Clifford Chance.

title: Automatic classification, extraction and summaries when a document is filed
problem: Version notes are rarely entered by hand, so search and AI summaries run on poorly described content, and scanned files can be invisible to search.
approach: On filing, the system classifies the document and extracts parties, dates and clauses; NetDocuments describes this in private preview for select customers.
iManage describes built-in text recognition so scanned files become searchable; no customer is named and no figure is published.
A lawyer or paralegal confirms extracted details, and the knowledge team samples machine-assigned labels.

title: Repository clean-up: AI finds duplicates and proposes reorganisation, applied after confirmation
problem: Teams store documents wherever is easiest, so nobody can say where all versions of a document are or which is latest.
approach: Digital Commerce Bank uses Ask iManage to find duplicates for librarians to file and delete; roughly 10 users now, 70 planned (vendor-published).
Harvey's Agentic Vault Organization (early access) proposes a folder or renaming plan, shows the changes, and acts only after a person confirms.
Librarians file and delete duplicates; a person confirms any proposed reorganisation.

title: Context graph mapping how matters, documents, communications and people connect
problem: Flat search finds passages, not relationships: an agent cannot tell which draft controls or that a counterparty is the same entity under another name.
approach: Platforms map relationships across documents, matters and the firm under existing permissions: NetDocuments (private preview), Harvey Graph, iManage and Wolters Kluwer.
Harvey: up to 30% better pass rate, up to about 50% cheaper tasks; NetDocuments: $0.68 to $0.36 per correct answer (vendor-published).
Answers stay verifiable through citations, and KM or IT reviews how the graph resolves matter and client boundaries.

title: Governed connections letting approved AI tools search firm knowledge and save work
problem: Lawyers use several AI products, and without a shared connection each needs its own integration or bulk export of firm content.
approach: The repository exposes an MCP server (an open connection standard) so approved tools search and save back under each user's permissions, logged.
Announced: Legora and a ChatGPT Enterprise plug-in with iManage; NetDocuments connections to Claude, Copilot, Harvey and others. No outcomes are published.
IT or KM approves which tools connect, and the lawyer reviews saved-back work before it becomes part of the record.

title: Agents with scoped, logged access that file work between review gates
problem: Filing documents, updating metadata and carrying matter context between steps are manual administrative tasks that agents could do but need safe access to.
approach: Agents act through a governed gateway under a person's permissions and audit logging; iManage says AI can draft, file and update metadata.
Harvey's Legal Work Orchestration lets agents run defined tasks while lawyers review at designated gates; announced, with no outcomes published.
Lawyers review at each gate before the next task starts, and agent permissions and logs are reviewed periodically.

title: Searchable precedent database built from the firm's deal history to benchmark terms
problem: Executed agreements hold what counterparties accepted, but relevant deals are spread across systems, so lawyers use generic examples or build comparison spreadsheets by hand.
approach: Ropes & Gray used generative AI to extract and compare historical deal terms into a searchable database for a private equity client.
Harvey's method: pick comparable deals, extract caps, baskets and survival periods into a review table, verify against citations. No measurement published.
The lawyer frames the question, chooses the comparable set and decides the negotiating position.

title: Curated, owned collections grounding AI, with senior review before entry
problem: AI answers are only as good as what they retrieve; stores mix drafts, executed deals and outdated templates, and nobody records why a document was judged final.
approach: Knowledge teams run a submit, enrich, publish, maintain and archive workflow for vetted precedents; Womble Bond Dickinson tags confidentiality and client.
McKinsey data stewards sanitise content for client confidentiality; context figures include 59% of organisations in the two earliest knowledge-management maturity stages (independent).
A KM lawyer or senior reviewer approves each asset before entry, and owners retire or refresh assets on a set cycle.
who: Womble Bond Dickinson, McKinsey, Draftwise, APQC

title: In-house legal knowledge base of standards and prior decisions for AI
problem: In-house legal teams hold years of documents and prior advice across fragmented systems; Rio Tinto's legal assets go back 20 years.
approach: BMW Group's legal function announced a Legora rollout with first drafts from approved standards; Rio Tinto moved 4.5 million documents to cloud.
Rio Tinto reports 80% adoption of the platform after four months, not an AI feature (vendor-published).
Legal decides what agents can handle, and lawyers verify prior advice retrieved by AI before relying on it.

title: In-house legal decisions captured as reusable positions, approved by an attorney
problem: In-house legal teams make thousands of judgment calls a year; the answer to the next similar request depends on which attorney picks it up.
approach: Coheso Memory, launched October 2026, proposes positions from resolved requests with reasoning, conditions and exceptions, and surfaces the precedent for similar requests.
Nothing takes effect until an attorney approves it; no outcomes are published (vendor-published).

title: Engagement lessons captured at close-out with AI-drafted retrospectives
problem: Lessons from finished engagements rarely reach the next team because writing them up is extra work at project close (an inference in the source).
approach: Project capture is automated into a searchable repository; Alvarez & Marsal, Simon-Kucher and AECOM described approaches at KMWorld Europe 2026.
Certinia and Kantata describe agents that draft retrospectives and organise lessons; no measurements are published.
The project lead and a responsible partner approve the retrospective, and the KM team checks for client-identifying detail.

title: AI call and meeting summaries as a knowledge source, within consent rules
problem: Know-how stays in conversation; meeting summaries could feed matter records and knowledge bases, but recording raises consent, confidentiality and tactical risks.
approach: AI tools record, transcribe and summarise calls so notes and decisions can be filed to the matter or knowledge base.
No outcomes are published (vendor-published).
The lawyer decides each time whether to record at all, and checks a summary before it is filed or shared.

title: Briefs from institutional memory for people joining a live matter
problem: A new team member on a complex matter spends time reconstructing context that already exists; Basware's customer success managers spent hours daily researching accounts.
approach: Chaffetz Lindsey attorneys use the document assistant to compare similar matters and bring a new team member up to speed.
Reported as days rather than weeks (vendor-published); Basware says managers regained four to five hours a day (vendor-published).
The matter lead reviews the brief, and the new team member still reads the key documents.

title: Knowledge teams curating the firm's AI know-how, tools, playbooks and gated rollout
problem: AI adoption is uneven: Troutman Pepper Locke noticed inconsistencies in who adopted AI and how much value they got, and 34% of professionals use unsanctioned AI.
approach: Troutman Pepper Locke curates approved tools, use cases and lessons in one repository; Lewis Silkin and Ropes & Gray use similar approaches.
Context figures: 57% of firms under 50 lawyers have a formal AI policy, rising to 98% at 350-699 (independent).
Practice-group knowledge partners decide which tools and playbooks become guidance, with periodic review of the approved-tool list.
who: Troutman Pepper Locke, Lewis Silkin, Ropes & Gray

title: Capturing senior judgment and reviewer corrections so juniors learn, with skill checks
problem: Judgment sits in senior people's heads, and in the accounting apprentice model juniors wait for busy season to end for a partner to explain changes.
approach: Ascend describes a closed loop where workflow traces and corrections feed its AI, plus a chat explaining what changed in a return.
A trial at eleven US IP firms found quality up 0.34 standard deviations at 10 days, skill retained at three months (vendor-published).
Partner review stays the source of explanation; periodic unaided exercises are recommended, and no firm is reported doing this.
who: Ascend, eleven US IP firms, Basware

title: AI twins that capture an individual professional's judgment for colleagues
problem: The most valuable knowledge is the context behind a document, which sits in emails, calls and memories and leaves when people retire.
approach: Twin1, launched August 2026, builds an AI twin per person from their work; its CEO says Linklaters, Orrick and Dechert use it.
No outcomes are published; the CEO's pipeline of more than 400 prospects is not an outcome (vendor-published).
The individual approves what their twin may say, and colleagues treat twin output as input to their own judgment.

title: Idea: structured capture of tacit know-how from people about to retire
problem: Idea, not a deployment: lessons-learned documents capture facts but not judgment, and senior professionals' tacit knowledge leaves with them.
approach: Practitioners discuss pairwise interviews, AI-supported story prototypes and a Tacit Knowledge Canvas; a KMWorld Europe 2026 workshop taught the method.
TechnipFMC built per-expert knowledge-transfer plans without AI; the Twin1 CEO says AI twins could help preserve partners' knowledge.
The expert approves the story or record of their judgment before it is shared.

title: Firm knowledge in a client-facing AI portal sold by subscription
problem: Clients want direct access to a firm's accumulated work, and one general counsel said law firms' AI use gives clients nothing and probably higher bills.
approach: Debevoise built STAAR on Legora, giving about 10 beta clients anonymised AI-risk documents and quoting approved text rather than synthesising.
Priced at $150,000 a year per subscription (self-reported); no usage, revenue or retention result reported.
A partner approves what enters the portal, and questions outside its scope go to lawyers.

title: Measuring the knowledge layer with search analytics, reuse measures and re-tests
problem: Firms spend more on knowledge management and AI but cannot show returns; APQC says knowledge management impact is hard to measure.
approach: Usage and reuse data is joined to matter and financial data; an unnamed global law firm plans analytics on search terms.
Firms re-run test sets of real questions when models change; in the Vals study, law firms contributed over 500 samples (independent).
KM and finance leaders agree metric definitions first, and a named owner signs off pass marks before go-live.
who: iManage, Vals, APQC; unnamed global law firm
